content:
GM fams 

I believe the new @axisrobotics Challenger Program is addressing a common issue with crowdsourced robot training

Not all contributions need to be for every task.

A simple pick and place task is quite a different challenge from a difficult articulated task such as drawers, cabinets or appliances.

You don't get a 'failed run' if someone who is inexperienced attempts the more difficult one. You may also end up with poor quality training data.

Now that Axis is moving those more challenging tasks to a different pool.

Access is based on a history of contributions, verification rate, pre and post training activity, task diversity, and consistency of performance relative to other people who are doing the same tasks.

The harder tasks are then assigned to qualified trainers, who will receive points that are 2-3 times as high per task.

I believe that configuration is good.

The more difficult tasks are assigned to those who have demonstrated their ability to create reliable trajectories, and new contributors are given a more forgiving method to learn.

The more data, the better it is for robot training.

It is even better if the right person is creating the right data.

That distinction is important.

content:
Humans Shouldn’t Do Everything

The Smartest Way to Train a Robot Might Be Knowing When to Step In. 

One thing about robotics training has been on my mind lately:

Does a human really need to control the robot from start to finish?

Probably not.

If a robot can already handle 80% of a task, having a human redo the entire trajectory just to fix the remaining 20% feels incredibly inefficient.

This is where @axisrobotics V2 gets interesting.

With its human-gated DAgger approach, the idea is simple:

Let the robot try.

Let it handle what it already knows.

And when it reaches a critical failure point, a human steps in and corrects it.

That small intervention can then become valuable training data.

So instead of collecting another long demonstration from scratch, the system focuses on the exact moment where the policy needs help.

I like this idea because it changes the role of the human.

The human isn’t replacing the robot.

They’re teaching it where it is still wrong.

And if those corrections keep feeding back into the training loop, every failure becomes an opportunity to reduce the need for human intervention next time.

That feels much closer to how scalable robot learning should work.

Don’t teach the robot everything.

Teach it what it still doesn’t know.

content:
The Missing Infrastructure Between AI Models and Robots

➜ Building a capable robot is not simply a matter of putting a powerful AI model inside a machine. A model needs physical experiences to understand how objects behave, how actions produce different outcomes, and how to respond when the real world does not behave exactly as expected.

➜ Those experiences require an entire infrastructure layer. Data must be generated through meaningful tasks, collected across different environments and embodiments, validated for quality, processed into useful formats and converted into training signals that models can actually learn from.

➜ The process does not stop once a model is trained. When a robot is evaluated in increasingly difficult situations, its failures reveal new weaknesses. Those failures can identify which tasks, environments or interactions require additional data, creating a continuous feedback loop between the robot and the data engine.

➜ This creates a larger Physical AI stack:

➜ Data → Models → Robots → Evaluation → Feedback → New Data

Each stage strengthens the next. Better data can improve models, better models can improve robotic performance, and real world failures can generate new requirements for the next generation of training data.

➜ This is the infrastructure thesis behind Axis Robotics. Axis is building systems for task generation, simulation data collection, egocentric data, real world data and data processing to help create the continuous flow of physical experiences that embodied AI needs.

➜ The important point is that the Physical AI stack is bigger than the robot and bigger than the model. Intelligence in machines requires an infrastructure layer that can continuously generate, refine and deliver useful physical experience.

➜ The long term advantage may belong to the platforms that can close this loop efficiently, turning robotic experience into better data, better data into better models, and better models into more capable machines.

Here is how @axisrobotics converts crowdsourced simulation on Axis Hub into general-purpose AI training data ↓

🔺 The Embodied AI Bottleneck Scaling physical automation requires internet-scale trajectory data. Gathering this data exclusively on physical hardware is slow, cost-prohibitive, and leaves models vulnerable to narrow, lab-specific environments.

🔺 Browser-Scale Teleoperation via Axis Hub Axis Hub moves teleoperation into standard web browsers using MuJoCo WebAssembly. Anyone can complete pick-and-place, pouring, and object manipulation tasks to generate structured spatial data without specialized hardware.

🔺 On-Chain Provenance on Base Every uploaded trajectory goes through automated sanity checks and VLM scoring. Verified runs receive an ungameable Data ID on Base, securing transparent contributor attribution and weekly epoch rewards.
  
🔺 Sim-to-Real Model Pipeline Verified trajectories are replayed through IsaacSim GPU clusters for photorealistic domain randomization. This multiplies human demonstrations into massive, high-diversity datasets that directly feed Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models.
 
Turn human interaction into the decentralized data engine for general-purpose physical AI.

Start contributing on Axis Hub ↓

But
content:
After exploring Axis Robotics for a few days, I found one thing quite interesting.

At first, I also thought it was primarily a platform for collecting data by having humans perform robot tasks.

But going a bit deeper, it turns out to be much bigger.

Because when a human performs a robot task, it doesn't automatically become useful training data.

Suppose you are doing a task.

If you pause in the middle, make minor errors in hand movement, or if there is noise in the trajectory these will inevitably exist in the raw data.

This is right where Axis's data pipeline caught my attention.

I was looking at their AxisDataCleaning GitHub repo. It includes processes like smoothing, resampling, metrics calculation, and offline task checking for raw trajectories.

Meaning, it's something like this:

- Human interaction     ↓
- Raw trajectory             ↓
- Cleaning                         ↓
- Task checking              ↓
- Better quality data     ↓
- Robot training

Just like in real life, simply recording a video doesn't make it the final video unnecessary parts must be cut first, the quality fixed, and then published.

It's pretty much the same idea for robot data.
And this is where Axis became interesting to me.
Because for Physical AI, you don't just need a lot of data.
You need good and usable data.

And if that can be created in a scalable way from the contributions of thousands of people, then the entire model of robotics data collection could change.

I no longer see Axis merely as a platform for doing robot tasks.
Rather human → interaction → verified data → robot learning

I see it as a part of this entire pipeline.

This is the most interesting aspect of Axis to me.

title:
I spent the night arguing with some friends about the nature of intelligence generally and specifically whether the AI labs are “building a God”. 

One argument was that if an LLM could call  tools th
content:
I spent the night arguing with some friends about the nature of intelligence generally and specifically whether the AI labs are “building a God”. 

One argument was that if an LLM could call  tools that enabled it to synthesize molecules an Agent could theoretically “create new forms of life”, eg bacteria with an entirely novel DNA sequence. Is that not God?

To which I said (maybe yelled lol), no. God creates Something from Nothing. An LLM does the opposite. It creates Something from Everything (in its training data). 

They are not Gods, they are a very efficient information processing tool. If you grant LLMs have a kind of intelligence, at best you can say that the labs have invented a kind of morally permissible slavery.

As the discussion unfolded, we all kind of came to the realization that the root of our diverging opinions was that I was the only parent at the table. And the experience of creating life so strongly shapes my beliefs about what LLMs are and are not. 

Another friend asked “well aren’t we just efficient information processing tools?”. And I just don’t know how any parent could say “people are just LLMs”.   

One can deny the existence of their own soul, but how could one look at their child and deny the existence of that ineffable spark that distinguishes man from machine?

法律を作らなくてもいい。

そこまで見ないと、これから何が起きるのかも分からない。

content:
Claude Opus、法律に詳しすぎる。

国税庁の質疑応答事例120問を、資料を渡さずに解かせたら、正解の条文を76.7%当てた。

更新前の「条文くん」の検索とは互角。しかも挙げた条文の99.4%は実在していた。

じゃあ、わざわざ検索して条文を渡す意味はあるのか。

ここを検証してみたら、条文を当てるだけでは見えなかった差があった。

今回、その検証結果をもとに、条文くんの検索エンジンを大幅アップデートしました。

ちなみに、このベンチマークの検証だけで10万円以上かかった。

条文くんは、渡した条文以外を引用できないホワイトリスト方式。今回の更新でもそこは変えておらず、実在しない条番号は出ない。

ただ、実在する条文だけを引けても、それで十分ではない。今回は正解条文を当てたかだけでなく、次の4要件で評価した。

正確性：引いた条文が実在し、今の問題に必要なものか。
無矛盾性：別制度の規範や、改正前後の規定を混ぜていないか。
十分性：答えに必要な規範が揃っているか。
必要最小性：結論に関係ない条文や、過剰に展開した参照先など、不要な資料を渡していないか。

判定はClaude Opus。税務の専門家による評価はまだ入れていない。

ベンチマーク構成での採点では、更新前後で比べると、

・別制度などを「混ぜない」
　68.3% → 80.0%

・必要な規範を「落とさない」
　71.8% → 76.5%

さらに、同じ生成モデルに資料を渡さず、AIの知識だけで答案を書かせた場合と比べると、

・別制度などを「混ぜない」
　条文くん80.0%／AIの知識だけ76.7%

・必要な規範を「落とさない」
　条文くん76.5%／AIの知識だけ66.6%

正確性と必要最小性には大きな差がない。差が出たのは、規範の混同と見落とし。必要な条文が手元にあることは、ここに効いていそうだった。

正解条文に到達した割合も、更新後の条文くんは83.5%になった。これは検索候補に入っただけではなく、選定して画面に出した段階の数字。

ただ、国税庁の公開問題は学習で見ている可能性がある。ほかの法令ではどうなのか。

そこで、税務とは別に、デジタル庁公開の法律4択問題集でも比較した。

正解条文に到達した割合は、
〈Claude Opusの知識だけ／条文くんの検索〉で、

・金融商品取引法：94.9%／100%
・薬機法：74.3%／100%
・借地借家法：100%／100%

借地借家法では並ぶ。一方、薬機法では約26ポイント差が出た。

知識だけでも十分に届く法令がある一方で、検索を組み合わせることで拾える条文もある。法令によって、その差がはっきり出た。

法律の回答は、書いてある条文が全部実在していても、必要な規範が1つ抜ければ結論が変わることがある。しかも、抜けているものは読む側も気づきにくい。

AIが知っている条文を確かめることに加えて、知識だけでは出てこない条文を、どう手元に届けるか。

今回の検証で、条文くんの検索を改善していく方向が、かなり具体的になった。

引き続き全力で頑張って参ります。

title: Senate Democrats urge Postal Service to halt implementation of new ballot restrictions
content: In a letter to Postmaster General David Steiner, the seven Democrats on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee (HSGAC) demanded Friday that the US Postal Service (USPS) halt implementation of new mail-ballot procedures required by President Donald Trump’s executive order. The senators also want answers about the legal authority for those new procedures no later than September 11, saying, “We reiterate our call to halt your breakneck implementation of the President’s unlawful order and rescind the final rule on federal ballot mail.” Trump issued Executive Order 14399 , “Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections,” on March 31. The order directs the Department of Homeland Security, in coordination with the Social Security Administration, to compile state lists of individuals confirmed to be US citizens who will be at least 18 and reside in the state. It separately directs USPS to establish requirements for mail-ballot envelopes, including agency approval and unique Intelligent Mail barcodes. USPS subsequently issued its final “Ballot Mail for Federal Elections” rule , which took effect August 21 and was published in the Federal Register August 26. A whistleblower disclosure received by HSGAC’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations alleged that the new systems risked “collapsing the absentee ballot system and disenfranchising millions of Americans” and described their development as a “seriously flawed, rushed, and chaotic process” undertaken without adequate testing or normal system standards. The whistleblower specifically alleged that if one barcode failed to scan in a batch of 10,000 ballots, the entire batch would be rejected and returned to the state. A USPS spokesperson told ProPublica that the agency was reviewing the whistleblower’s concerns and had spent months developing the system in a manner consistent with court orders. The letter sets a deadline of September 1
author: Brendan Hickey | Vermont Law & Graduate School, US

title: UN experts call on Honduras to halt evictions of peasant, Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities
content: A group of UN experts called on Honduras Friday to immediately halt evictions of peasant, Indigenous, and Afro-descendant communities under Decree No. 107-2026 , also known as the Law for the Strengthening and Protection of the Agro-Industrial Sector, Energy Projects, Tourism, Livestock, and Small Agricultural Producers. The experts said: “We cannot stand by and watch the deliberate closing of every legal door through which a peasant, Indigenous or Afro-descendant family in Honduras can challenge dispossession.” The decree declares specified projects to be of national interest, expedites administrative procedures, and directs authorities to act against occupations and blockades. It states that it does not apply in recognized Indigenous and tribal territories without free, prior, and informed consultation. The experts nevertheless argued that the law could allow companies to obtain land cultivated by cooperatives and local farmers without agrarian review or adequate consideration of ancestral territorial claims. The experts also warned that the decree could conflict with Honduras’ obligation to respect, protect, and fulfill the right to food . They said dispossessing communities of land essential to their food security would undermine access to productive resources. They further condemned evictions carried out by Honduran authorities on July 6, including an operation affecting the Garífuna community of San Juan in Tela. According to Amnesty International , five members of the Black Fraternal Organization of Honduras were arrested during the operation and now face charges of aggravated usurpation related to their defense of the community’s ancestral territory. author: Salma Ben Mariem | Faculty of Law and Political Science of Sousse, TN

title: Death of Baloch student raises concerns amid enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings, UN experts say
content: UN experts on Friday have raised alarm over the alleged enforced disappearance, torture, and extrajudicial killing of Imran Ali, a student from the Balochistan province, calling it part of a state-sponsored pattern of targeting ethnic Baloch people and urged Pakistan to conduct an urgent investigation. In commenting on the importance of transparency and accountability in shedding light on the circumstances surrounding Imran Ali’s death, the experts stated: The enforced disappearance of Imran Ali and his death in custody must be subject to a prompt, thorough, independent, and impartial investigation. Such an investigation must include independent forensic examinations, proper identification of the body, and its dignified return to the family. It should establish the cause, manner, and circumstances of Ali’s death, while identifying those responsible, with a view to ensuring accountability. In late August 2025, Ali was kidnapped from his residence by around 20 agents from the Counter-Terrorism Department before being subsequently taken to a secret location. His fate and precise location remained a mystery for a year, leading to a period of agonizing uncertainty for his family. However, former detainees who were in captivity with him confirmed that he often endured periods of torture by personnel from the Counter-Terrorism Department, a measure that directly contravenes Article 2 of the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment and Article 7 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. His fate only came to light approximately a year after he went missing, when a police officer testified before a hearing before Pakistan’s Commission of Inquiry on Enforced Disappearances saying that Ali had lost his life in May 2026, but due to delays by authorities in properly identifying his body and the alleged inability to preserve his remains, he was later buried. title: Texas and Florida Step Back from ALPRs
content: Within the last few days, two important state actions have dealt a big blow to automated license plate reader (ALPR) networks. This is just the latest proof of the growing tide of public opposition to mass surveillance. After years of successful grassroots battles to pull these cameras from local streets, bipartisan momentum is sweeping the country. On August 28, Texas Governor Greg Abbott banned state agencies from spending public funds on Flock cameras . The order dropped just as The Texas Tribune prepared to publish an investigation revealing that a state agency had quietly funneled at least $30 million into building a sprawling surveillance network. Then on August 31, the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) issued a memo , announced by Governor Ron DeSantis, ordering the removal of all ALPRs from the right-of-way on state highways within 30 days. The order revokes all previously approved permits to install ALPRs, and bars transportation officials from issuing future permits. FDOT officials stated that “the recent exponential increase in deployments along our roadways, coupled with concerning reports of misuse, data privacy concerns, and surveillance schemes merit immediate action to preserve Floridians’ sovereignty and quality of life.” FDOT’s action has been followed by a surge of local governments in Florida canceling or pausing their vendor contracts . Much more work remains. Many ALPRs in Florida are not on state highways, but sit on city streets, county roads, residential driveways, and shopping center parking lots—and FDOT's order doesn't touch any of them. Likewise, the Texas directive leaves local agencies free to use city, county, federal, and private funds to install cameras. This week’s good news follows years of pushback from local advocates that has seen dozens of cities sever ties with surveillance companies.
